q: All doctors in a certain hospital wear white coats. Dr Ali is a doctor in that hospital. Which statement must be true?
o: Everyone who wears a white coat is a doctor
Dr Ali is the only doctor in the hospital
Nurses in the hospital do not wear white coats
Dr Ali wears a white coat
x: Dr Ali belongs to the group 'doctors in the hospital', and every member of that group wears a white coat. The statements say nothing about other people who wear white coats or about nurses.

q: Every student in Section Blue passed the test. Sara did not pass the test. Which statement must be true?
o: Sara is in Section Blue
Some students in Section Blue failed the test
The test was too difficult for Sara
Sara is not in Section Blue
x: If Sara were in Section Blue she would have passed, because every student there passed. She did not pass, so she cannot be in that section.

q: If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was not cancelled. Which statement must be true?
o: It did not rain
It rained
The match was played in the evening
The match is cancelled only when it rains
x: Rain would have led to cancellation. Since there was no cancellation, there was no rain. The statements do not say rain is the only reason for cancelling a match.

q: If Hamza studies, he passes. Hamza passed. What can be concluded with certainty about whether Hamza studied?
o: Nothing certain: he may or may not have studied
Hamza definitely studied
Hamza definitely did not study
Hamza will pass every future test
x: The rule says studying leads to passing; it does not say passing happens only after studying. Hamza could have passed for another reason, so we cannot be sure he studied.

q: Some P are Q. All Q are R. Which statement must be true?
o: All P are R
Some P are R
Some R are not P
No P is R
x: The P that are Q are also R, because every Q is R. So at least some P are R. Nothing tells us about the P that are not Q, so 'All P are R' is not certain.

q: Every shop on Mall Road closes by 9 pm every day. Bilal's shop is on Mall Road. Which statement CANNOT be true?
o: Bilal's shop closes at 8 pm
Some shops on other roads stay open after 9 pm
Bilal's shop was open at 10 pm last Monday
Bilal also owns a second shop on another road that closes at 11 pm
x: Bilal's Mall Road shop must close by 9 pm every day, so it could not be open at 10 pm on Monday. The other statements do not contradict the given facts.

q: No fruit in the basket is rotten. Some fruits in the basket are mangoes. Which statement must be true?
o: Some mangoes are not rotten
No mango anywhere is rotten
All the fruits in the basket are mangoes
Some mangoes in the basket are rotten
x: The mangoes in the basket are fruits in the basket, and none of those is rotten. So at least these mangoes are not rotten. Mangoes outside the basket are not covered by the statements.

q: Ayesha is taller than Fatima. Fatima is taller than Zainab. Hira is shorter than Ayesha. Which statement must be true?
o: Ayesha is taller than Zainab
Hira is taller than Fatima
Hira is shorter than Zainab
Fatima is the shortest of the four
x: Ayesha > Fatima > Zainab, so Ayesha is taller than Zainab. Hira is only known to be shorter than Ayesha, so her place compared with Fatima and Zainab is unknown.

q: Every member of the debating club also belongs to the library club. Usman is a member of the debating club. Which statement CANNOT be true?
o: Usman is not a member of the library club
Some library club members are not in the debating club
Usman is also a member of the cricket club
Usman joined the library club before the debating club
x: Being in the debating club means being in the library club, so Usman must be in the library club. The other statements could all be true without breaking the given rule.

q: Which fact shows that the claim 'All birds can fly' is false?
o: The bat can fly but is not a bird
Many birds fly very long distances
The ostrich is a bird that cannot fly
Some insects can fly
x: A claim about 'all birds' is disproved by one bird that cannot fly, and the ostrich is such a bird. A flying bat or insect says nothing about whether every bird flies.

q: Everyone in the college team is a cricketer. Which extra statement, if true, makes the conclusion 'Ali is a cricketer' certain?
o: Ali likes cricket
All cricketers in the college are in the team
Ali watches every match of the team
Ali is in the college team
x: If Ali is in the team, the rule 'everyone in the team is a cricketer' applies to him. 'All cricketers are in the team' reverses the rule and does not tell us about Ali.

q: At least one of these is true: the printer is out of ink, or the printer is switched off. The printer is switched on. Which statement must be true?
o: The printer has plenty of ink
The printer is out of ink
The printer is broken
The printer is switched off
x: One of the two conditions must hold. Since the printer is not switched off, the other condition, being out of ink, must be true.

q: If the shop is open, its lights are on. If its lights are on, the guard is present. The guard is not present. Which statement must be true?
o: The lights are on
The shop is not open
The shop is open
The guard has gone home early
x: No guard means the lights are not on (second rule), and lights off means the shop is not open (first rule). Why the guard is absent cannot be known.

q: All P are Q. No Q is R. Which statement must be true?
o: Some P are R
All Q are P
Some R are P
No P is R
x: Every P lies inside Q, and Q shares nothing with R, so P shares nothing with R either. 'All Q are P' is not certain, since Q may contain things that are not P.

q: Whenever it rains, Sana takes the bus to college. Today it rained and Sana went to college. Which statement CANNOT be true?
o: Sana took the bus to college today
Sana walked all the way to college today
Sana sometimes takes the bus on dry days
Sana reached college late today
x: On a rainy day Sana always takes the bus, so she cannot have walked all the way. The rule says nothing about dry days or about her arrival time.

q: In a class of 30 students, 18 study Biology and 20 study Chemistry. Every student studies at least one of these two subjects. Which statement must be true?
o: Exactly 10 students study both subjects
At least 12 students study both subjects
Exactly 8 students study both subjects
No student studies both subjects
x: 18 + 20 = 38 places for 30 students, so 38 − 30 = 8 students are counted twice. As every student studies at least one subject, exactly 8 study both.

q: Statement: Should wearing a helmet be compulsory for motorcyclists? Argument I: Yes, helmets reduce head injuries in road accidents. Argument II: No, helmets spoil people's hairstyles.
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives an important, directly relevant reason about safety. Argument II is trivial compared with the safety issue, so it is weak.

q: Statement: Should students get a short break between two long lectures? Argument I: Yes, a short break helps students stay attentive. Argument II: Yes, because every other college does it.
o: Only argument II is strong
Only argument I is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a real reason linked to learning. Argument II only says others do it, which is an appeal to popularity and gives no reason of its own.

q: Statement: Should all private cars be banned in big cities to reduce pollution? Argument I: No, this would badly affect people who have no other way to travel. Argument II: Yes, this would completely end all pollution in cities.
o: Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I points to a real and serious problem the ban would cause. Argument II is an exaggeration: cars are not the only source of pollution, so a ban could not end all of it.

q: Statement: Should the government open more medical colleges? Argument I: Yes, the country needs more doctors for its population. Argument II: No, new colleges without trained teachers and hospitals would lower the quality of training.
o: Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
x: Both arguments are relevant and serious: one points to the shortage of doctors, the other to the risk of poor training. Each is a strong argument from its own side.

q: Statement: Should mobile phones be banned for everyone under 18? Argument I: Yes, young people never use phones for anything useful. Argument II: No, because every country in the world allows them.
o: Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
x: Argument I is a sweeping overgeneralisation ('never'). Argument II relies on what others do and is not even known to be true. Neither gives a sound reason.

q: Ali says: "I will catch the 7 o'clock train so that I reach Lahore in time for my interview." Which assumption is Ali making?
o: The interview will be cancelled
The train is the cheapest way to travel
Ali has visited Lahore before
The 7 o'clock train will reach Lahore before the interview
x: Ali's plan makes sense only if that train arrives before the interview starts. Cost and past visits play no part in his reasoning.

q: An advertisement says: "Use Brightex toothpaste for whiter teeth." Which assumption does the advertisement make?
o: Brightex is the cheapest toothpaste
Some people want whiter teeth
All other toothpastes damage teeth
Everyone already uses Brightex
x: An advert offering whiter teeth is pointless unless people want whiter teeth. It does not compare price or claim that other toothpastes cause harm.

q: The principal announces: "From next week the library will stay open until 8 pm so that students can study there after classes." Which assumption does this decision rest on?
o: All students live near the college
Some students will use the library after classes
Students cannot study at home at all
The library has too few books
x: Keeping the library open later is useful only if some students will actually come. The decision does not need every student to live nearby or be unable to study at home.

q: "Sara got the highest marks in the class, so she must have studied for more hours than anyone else." Which hidden assumption does this argument depend on?
o: Sara enjoys studying
No other student took the test
Marks depend only on the number of hours studied
Sara's teacher favours her
x: The jump from highest marks to most hours works only if hours of study alone decide marks. In fact, understanding and study methods also matter, so the argument is weak.

q: Claim: "Regular exercise improves sleep." Which fact gives the most valid support for this claim?
o: Many famous athletes say they sleep well
Sales of exercise machines have risen
Some people prefer to exercise in the evening
People who began daily walks fell asleep faster than before, while a similar group who did not change their routine showed no change
x: Only the first fact compares people who exercised with similar people who did not, so it links the change in sleep to exercise. Celebrity opinions and sales figures are not evidence about sleep.

q: Which is a reason based on evidence, rather than opinion, for believing that a new medicine works?
o: A famous actor recommends the medicine
The medicine has been sold for many years
Its packet says it is very powerful
In a fair trial, patients given the medicine recovered faster than similar patients given a dummy pill
x: A fair comparison with a dummy pill tests the medicine directly. Recommendations, long sales and packet claims are not evidence that it works.

q: Statement: Should the school day start an hour later in winter? Argument I: Yes, early winter mornings are foggy and cold, making travel to school unsafe for young children. Argument II: No, a later start would make school end later, leaving less daylight for children to get home.
o: Only argument I is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument II is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Both arguments are relevant and concern children's safety: fog in the morning against darkness in the evening. Each is a strong argument from its own side.

q: A notice in a building says: "In case of fire, use the stairs, not the lift." Which assumption does the notice make?
o: Stairs are always faster than a lift
Fires happen only in tall buildings
The lift may be unsafe to use during a fire
Nobody ever uses the lift
x: The advice only makes sense if the lift could be dangerous during a fire. It does not claim stairs are always faster or that fires happen only in tall buildings.

q: "All students who passed the entry test were admitted. Hamza was admitted. So Hamza passed the entry test." Which added statement would make this conclusion certain?
o: Hamza is a hard-working student
Every student who applied passed the entry test
Only students who passed the entry test were admitted
The entry test was easy
x: As stated, the argument reverses the rule: passing led to admission, but others might also have been admitted. If only those who passed were admitted, Hamza's admission proves he passed.

q: Which is the strongest reason for believing that the earth is round rather than flat?
o: Most people say the earth is round
Classroom globes are round
A ship sailing away seems to sink from the bottom up as it goes over the horizon
Ancient maps were drawn on flat paper
x: A ship's hull disappearing before its mast is an observation explained by a curved surface. Popular opinion and the shape of globes or maps are not evidence.

q: Fatima believes that drinking boiled water lowers the risk of typhoid. Which is a valid reason for her belief?
o: Her grandmother told her so
Boiled water tastes different
Most of her neighbours drink boiled water
Boiling kills most of the germs that spread water-borne diseases such as typhoid
x: Typhoid spreads through germs in contaminated water, and boiling kills such germs. What relatives or neighbours say or do, or a change in taste, is not a reason.

q: Ahmed met two rude shopkeepers in a city and concluded that all shopkeepers in that city are rude. Which error in reasoning is this?
o: Hasty generalisation
Appeal to popularity
Attacking the person instead of the argument
Circular reasoning
x: Ahmed draws a conclusion about all shopkeepers from only two cases. A conclusion from too few examples is a hasty generalisation.

q: "This shampoo must be the best because millions of people use it." What is wrong with this reasoning?
o: It draws a conclusion from too few examples
It treats a correlation as a cause
It treats popularity as proof of quality
It attacks the person making the claim
x: Many users do not prove that a product is the best; people may choose it for price or advertising. This is the appeal to popularity.

q: "Ice-cream sales and cases of drowning both rise in summer, so eating ice-cream causes drowning." Which flaw does this argument contain?
o: It takes a correlation as proof of causation
It appeals to popularity
It attacks the person instead of the argument
It uses circular reasoning
x: The two rise together because hot weather increases both ice-cream eating and swimming. Moving together does not show that one causes the other.

q: Hamza wore his blue shirt on the day he passed an exam, so he now believes the shirt brings him luck. What is the error in his belief?
o: Accepting a claim because many people believe it
Assuming that because one thing came before an event, it caused the event
Attacking a person instead of the argument
Repeating the claim as its own reason
x: The shirt was simply worn before the result; nothing links it to his marks. Taking 'came before' to mean 'caused' is a false-cause error.

q: Sara argues that the college canteen should sell fresh fruit. Bilal replies, "Don't listen to her, she failed her maths test." Why is Bilal's reply weak?
o: It is based on a large survey
It appeals to the popularity of fruit
It confuses a correlation with a cause
It attacks Sara instead of answering her argument
x: Sara's maths result has nothing to do with whether the canteen should sell fruit. Bilal attacks the person rather than dealing with her reason.

q: "Our teacher is always right because she never makes mistakes." What is wrong with this argument?
o: The reason only repeats the claim in other words
It draws a conclusion from too few examples
It relies on what most people believe
It treats a correlation as a cause
x: 'Never makes mistakes' means the same as 'always right', so no new support is given. This is circular reasoning.

q: A researcher asked 20 people at a gym whether they exercise regularly; 19 said yes. She concluded that 95% of people in the city exercise regularly. What is the main flaw?
o: 19 out of 20 is not equal to 95%
The researcher relied on an appeal to authority
People at a gym are not typical of everyone in the city
The survey mixed up a cause and an effect
x: 19 out of 20 is indeed 95%, but people found at a gym are far more likely to exercise than the average citizen. The sample does not represent the city.

q: Towns with more hospitals record more deaths each year. Someone concludes that hospitals cause deaths. Which fact best exposes the flaw?
o: Bigger towns have both more hospitals and more people, so more deaths
Hospitals employ trained doctors
Some small villages have no hospital at all
Deaths are recorded by the government
x: Population size raises both the number of hospitals and the number of deaths. A third factor explains the link, so hospitals need not be the cause.

q: "Either you score full marks or you are a complete failure." Why is this a false belief?
o: It attacks the person instead of the idea
It relies on what most people believe
It ignores the many results between the two extremes
It treats a correlation as a cause
x: Scores can fall anywhere between full marks and failure. Offering only two choices when many exist is a false either-or.

q: "A famous cricketer says this herbal powder cures diabetes, so it must work." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
o: The cricketer is very popular
The herbal powder is costly
Diabetes is a common disease
The cricketer is not an expert on medicine, and his word is not evidence
x: Fame in sport gives no expertise in medicine. A claim about a cure needs evidence from proper testing, not a celebrity's word.

q: Which is an example of a hasty generalisation?
o: After tasting one sour orange from a cart, Ayesha decides every orange in the market is sour
After weighing every bag in a delivery, a clerk says all the bags weigh 10 kg
After reading the full timetable, Bilal says all classes start at 8 am
After counting every student, Zainab says there are 40 in the room
x: Ayesha judges a whole market from one orange. The others check every case before concluding, so their conclusions are safe.

q: Students who sit in the front row get higher marks on average, so a writer claims that sitting in front raises marks. Which fact, if true, most weakens the claim?
o: Front-row seats are closest to the board
The classroom has six rows of seats
Hard-working students tend to choose front-row seats
Marks are given out of 100
x: If hard-working students pick the front row, their effort could explain the higher marks rather than the seat. Being close to the board would support the claim, not weaken it.

q: Bilal says, "I have never seen a germ, so germs do not exist." Why is this a false belief?
o: Germs exist only in hospitals
Not having seen something is not proof that it does not exist
Most people believe that germs exist
Bilal is too young to judge
x: Germs are too small to see without a microscope, so failing to see them proves nothing. Lack of personal observation is not evidence of absence.

q: "This remedy is made only from plants, so it cannot have any harmful effects." Why is this belief false?
o: Being natural does not make something safe; some plants contain harmful substances
Plants grow slowly
Most people prefer plant remedies
Plant remedies are cheaper than tablets
x: Whether a substance is safe depends on what it contains and how much is taken, not on whether it comes from a plant. Some plants are poisonous.

q: "Ten students who drank green tea got good marks, so green tea improves marks." Which question would best test this claim?
o: How much does green tea cost?
Did similar students who did not drink green tea get lower marks?
Did the ten students enjoy the tea?
Which shop sold the tea?
x: A cause can only be judged by comparing with a similar group who did not drink the tea. Without that comparison, the good marks may have nothing to do with tea.
